title: First 10 Minutes
label: Getting started
lead: Run the cross-agent proof, explore the demo, onboard a real local workspace, seed your current repo, add one source, save one explicit memory, then ask an agent to query Link through MCP, skills, or the CLI.

sections.heading: 1. Prove The Memory Loop
sections.text: Start with lnk proof . It creates a clean local workspace, writes one reviewed memory, then recalls it through the same bounded path used by CLI, skills, and MCP. This proves the core product before you configure an…
sections.body: Start with lnk proof . It creates a clean local workspace, writes one reviewed memory, then recalls it through the same bounded path used by CLI, skills, and MCP. This proves the core product before you configure an agent or open the web viewer. macOS with Homebrew: brew install gowtham0992/link/link lnk proof You should see Cross-agent memory continuity works and Result: proof passed . The richer demo is next. It already has raw sources, wiki pages, memories, backlinks, graph data, and a local viewer to inspect: lnk try lnk serve link-demo The Homebrew formula is maintained in the public gowtham0992/homebrew-link tap. Or from source: git clone https://github.com/gowtham0992/link.git cd link python3 link.py proof python3 link.py demo python3 link.py next link-demo python3 link.py serve link-demo On Windows from source, use the Python launcher: git clone https://github.com/gowtham0992/link.git cd link py link.py proof py link.py demo py link.py next link-demo py link.py serve link-demo lnk try creates the demo, checks readiness, runs a compact query and brief, and prints the viewer command plus the first agent prompts. From source, use python3 link.py try or py link.py try . Judge the generated demo The repo's root wiki/ is only a scaffold for local development and personal testing. Generated content in wiki/ , raw/ , and link-demo/ is ignored by git so private memory is not published by accident. Viewer is optional lnk serve is only for browsing Link in a local web UI. CLI commands, official skills, and MCP-enabled agents work without it because they read the same local wiki/ files directly. The demo includes one pending memory intentionally, so the review inbox and explain-memory workflow are visible. Run lnk review-memory prefer-local-personal-memory link-demo if you want memory audit to be fully clear. Open http://127.0.0.1:3000 , then inspect /onboard , /brief , /memory , /ingest , /graph , and /health . Open more for prompts, proposal review, audit, captures, profile, log, and all pages. Link accepts localhost too, but the numeric loopback address avoids slow IPv6 fallback in some Safari setups. lnk start link-demo --task "working on agent memory" lnk query "why does Link help agents?" link-demo --budget small lnk brief "working on agent memory" link-demo lnk benchmark "agent memory" link-demo lnk health link-demo

sections.heading: 2. Make It Yours — One Command
sections.text: lnk setup is install day and every upgrade after it: it detects every agent installed on your machine — Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Windsurf, Zed, Kiro, Gemini CLI and Antigravity — and wires them all at once: workspace…
sections.body: lnk setup is install day and every upgrade after it: it detects every agent installed on your machine — Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Windsurf, Zed, Kiro, Gemini CLI and Antigravity — and wires them all at once: workspace create/repair, MCP provisioning, hooks for agents that have them, and a refresh of the global instruction files you chose with lnk compile --global (it names the agents that could use one, but never creates one). It is idempotent, so after any brew upgrade you just run it again. lnk setup # every detected agent, wired lnk setup --preview # show the plan without writing agent configs Prefer the guided single-agent flow? lnk onboard checks health, prints the first agent prompts, and previews MCP wiring without changing agent config files unless you pass --write . lnk onboard lnk onboard --first-memory "I prefer concise release notes" lnk onboard --seed-project . lnk onboard --agent codex lnk onboard --agent codex --write lnk onboard --agent claude-code --hooks --write From source, use python3 link.py onboard on macOS/Linux or py link.py onboard on Windows. The command is safe to re-run: it preserves existing wiki data and only applies safe structural repairs. Add --seed-project . from inside a repo when you want onboarding to create the first source-backed project page. If the local viewer is running, http://127.0.0.1:3000/onboard shows the same setup loop with copy buttons.

sections.heading: 3. Seed Project Context
sections.text: Run lnk seed inside a project so Link has useful source-backed context before you ask an agent to recall anything. It reads allowlisted project files such as README.md , AGENTS.md , CLAUDE.md , .cursorrules , and editor…
sections.body: Run lnk seed inside a project so Link has useful source-backed context before you ask an agent to recall anything. It reads allowlisted project files such as README.md , AGENTS.md , CLAUDE.md , .cursorrules , and editor rule files, blocks secret-looking values, writes a generated source page, and rebuilds the graph. cd /path/to/your/project lnk seed . ~/link lnk query "what is this project about?" ~/link --budget small Seeding does not create durable memories. It gives agents a cited project source to retrieve from; preferences and decisions should still go through reviewed memory proposals.

sections.heading: 4. Install Link For Your Agent (source checkouts)
sections.text: Skip this if you ran lnk setup : it already wired every agent it found. From a cloned checkout, the installers add the agent's instruction block and then call lnk connect --write for the MCP entry (plus hooks for the…
sections.body: Skip this if you ran lnk setup : it already wired every agent it found. From a cloned checkout, the installers add the agent's instruction block and then call lnk connect --write for the MCP entry (plus hooks for the agents that have them), which verifies the runtime, creates the config if it does not exist, and edits JSON-with-comments settings without losing comments. Re-running an installer updates code and instructions without replacing existing wiki data. The matching uninstall.sh calls lnk disconnect --write , which removes Link's MCP entry and hooks and nothing else. bash integrations/codex/install.sh bash integrations/kiro/install.sh bash integrations/claude-code/install.sh bash integrations/cursor/install.sh bash integrations/copilot/install.sh bash integrations/vscode/install.sh bash integrations/antigravity/install.sh Use --project for a repo-local Link install. Project-scoped memory then stays separate from other project memory while still allowing broad user memory to be recalled. On Windows PowerShell, use the matching install.ps1 script. The PowerShell installers add the instruction block and scaffold the workspace but do not call lnk connect or install hooks, so run lnk connect <agent> ~/link --hooks --write after one: .\integrations\codex\install.ps1 .\integrations\kiro\install.ps1 .\integrations\claude-code\install.ps1 .\integrations\cursor\install.ps1 .\integrations\copilot\install.ps1 .\integrations\vscode\install.ps1 .\integrations\antigravity\install.ps1

sections.heading: 5. Add One Source
sections.text: Open the local viewer and use ingest -> Add Raw Source , or write a first note directly: mkdir -p ~/link/raw cat > ~/link/raw/first-memory.md <<'EOF' --- title: "First Link memory" source_type: note date_captured:…
sections.body: Open the local viewer and use ingest -> Add Raw Source , or write a first note directly: mkdir -p ~/link/raw cat > ~/link/raw/first-memory.md <<'EOF' --- title: "First Link memory" source_type: note date_captured: 2026-05-04 --- # First Link memory I am testing Link as local personal memory for agents. Raw notes stay local. The agent turns them into source-cited wiki pages. EOF Check pending work: lnk ingest-status Safety gate Link blocks normal ingest guidance when raw files contain secret-looking values or cannot be read safely. Redact or fix those local files first. Existing Link data If you already have files in ~/link/raw/ , lnk ingest-status may point to a different pending file first. If first-memory.md was already ingested and you overwrite it, Link marks that raw file as stale and asks the agent to refresh the existing source page.

sections.text: Use natural language with an agent: remember that I am testing Link as local personal memory for agents start with Link before we continue what does Link remember about local personal memory? CLI-first agents or Link…

sections.heading: 7. Ask The Agent To Ingest
sections.text: In your agent chat, ask: ingest raw/first-memory.md into Link The agent reads ~/link/LINK.md , creates a source page, updates concepts/entities when useful, updates the index and log, rebuilds backlinks, and validates…
sections.body: In your agent chat, ask: ingest raw/first-memory.md into Link The agent reads ~/link/LINK.md , creates a source page, updates concepts/entities when useful, updates the index and log, rebuilds backlinks, and validates generated pages. Return to /ingest after the agent finishes. Link shows which raw files are represented and gives follow-up prompts for proposals or retrieval checks.

sections.text: lnk doctor --fix lnk health lnk ingest-status lnk validate lnk memory-audit lnk operations lnk verify-mcp lnk verify-mcp should report Result: ready when you use MCP. Then ask your agent: query Link for first Link…
sections.body: lnk doctor --fix lnk health lnk ingest-status lnk validate lnk memory-audit lnk operations lnk verify-mcp lnk verify-mcp should report Result: ready when you use MCP. Then ask your agent: query Link for first Link memory If the answer comes from Link, local agent memory is working.

sections.heading: 9. Make The Loop Automatic (Session Hooks)
sections.text: Agents with session-hook support — Claude Code and Cursor, and for the session-start brief Codex, Gemini CLI, Antigravity and Copilot — can run the memory loop without being asked. --hooks installs hooks that inject a…
sections.body: Agents with session-hook support — Claude Code and Cursor, and for the session-start brief Codex, Gemini CLI, Antigravity and Copilot — can run the memory loop without being asked. --hooks installs hooks that inject a bounded memory brief at the start of every new session and store proposal-only session notes at session end. Empty sessions are skipped, duplicate end events are deduplicated, and durable memory still requires your approval. When the review backlog grows, the injected brief nudges the agent to offer a read-only lnk consolidate pass. On Claude Code the hooks also run before shell and file tool calls: a reviewed memory\'s enforced rules are checked there (asking for your OK or blocking), and memories anchored to the file being read or edited are surfaced at that moment. The same rule checks run on Cursor, Codex, Gemini CLI, Antigravity, Copilot and Windsurf, each through its own hook; where an agent can only allow or block, an ask rule holds the call until you approve it once with lnk approve <id> or in LinkBar. lnk receipt shows what actually arrived in each session. lnk connect claude-code ~/link --hooks --write lnk connect codex ~/link --hooks --write # session-start brief (Codex has no session-end event) lnk connect cursor ~/link --hooks --write Hook support beyond Claude Code is new in 6.0 and follows each vendor's documented hook schema; enforcement is measured on one live Codex session and by replaying recorded tool calls through the installed hook; a live Claude Code session has not been benchmarked yet. If a hook misbehaves on another agent, please open an issue.

sections.heading: 10. Optional: LinkBar, the menu bar app (macOS)
sections.text: Hooks make capture automatic; LinkBar makes reviewing it ambient. It puts the review gate in your menu bar: proposals arrive as a native notification with a one-tap Accept , a global palette ( ⌥⌘M ) recalls or remembers…
sections.body: Hooks make capture automatic; LinkBar makes reviewing it ambient. It puts the review gate in your menu bar: proposals arrive as a native notification with a one-tap Accept , a global palette ( ⌥⌘M ) recalls or remembers from any app, a live pulse shows which agent sessions are writing right now, and a Status tab reports the health of every Link surface (CLI, workspace, MCP, hooks, recall tier, viewer) with one-click fixes. It runs the same reviewed lnk commands you just wired — nothing new to trust. brew install --cask gowtham0992/link/linkbar LinkBar ships unsigned (no Apple Developer certificate); the cask clears the quarantine flag on install so it opens like any other app. Prefer building it yourself: cd apps/LinkBar && bash Scripts/bundle.sh --install .

sections.heading: 11. Optional: Hybrid Semantic Recall
sections.text: Lexical recall is always the default and the fallback. Two optional local tiers add paraphrase recall — "how should I structure my pull requests" finds a memory about commit style. The models load offline-only at recall…
sections.body: Lexical recall is always the default and the fallback. Two optional local tiers add paraphrase recall — "how should I structure my pull requests" finds a memory about commit style. The models load offline-only at recall time (a query can never trigger a download), embeddings are plain JSON under .link-cache/ , and there is no vector database or service. lnk semantic ~/link --setup # installs the extras if needed + fetches the models once python3 -m link_mcp --semantic-setup --wiki ~/link/wiki # MCP-only installs On Homebrew installs the runtime Python refuses direct pip install s (PEP 668), so --setup provisions the extras into Link's managed venv ( ~/.link-mcp-venv ) automatically — the same venv the MCP server runs from, and lnk uses it on the next command. In your own venv, pip install "link-mcp[semantic]" (fast tier) or "link-mcp[semantic-quality]" (quality tier) works as usual before running --setup . Recall quality is measured, not asserted: see benchmarks/RESULTS.md for the full methodology, numbers, and honest limitations.

sections.heading: 12. The Three Questions Everyone Asks
sections.text: Does Link read my conversations? Link never sees a conversation. The session hooks do the reading: at session end the agent's own transcript is mined locally and deterministically — no LLM, no network — for statements…
sections.body: Does Link read my conversations? Link never sees a conversation. The session hooks do the reading: at session end the agent's own transcript is mined locally and deterministically — no LLM, no network — for statements that look like durable preferences or decisions ("from now on I only push to develop"). Those become proposals in a pending inbox. Nothing is memory until you approve it, and the whole pipeline runs from plain Python files inside your own workspace that you can read ( link_core/agent_hooks.py ). If you never install hooks, Link only knows what you explicitly tell it with lnk remember . What happens when I clear context or open a new terminal? That is the whole point of Link. Context windows are disposable — cleared, compacted, abandoned with every new terminal. Your memory does not live there: it lives in Markdown files under ~/link , outside every context window. When a new session starts, the hook injects a compact brief of relevant memories back in; when an agent needs more, it asks over MCP. Clear context a hundred times — the agent still knows you never push to main, because that fact was never in the context to begin with. It was in a file. Which project or branch does a memory belong to? Every memory carries an explicit scope — user (true everywhere: "I prefer concise release notes") or project (tied to one repo: "this service deploys from tags"). Project memories are labeled with their project and don't leak into other repos' briefs. For finer fencing, applies_when conditions ( project: , path: , task: ) demote a memory to out of context — verify whenever you're outside its territory — so one project's conventions never masquerade as another's. Old checkouts and stale branches can't pollute recall: it's deterministic frontmatter you can open and edit, not classifier guesswork. title: Why Link?
label: Why Link
lead: The wiki is the inspectable storage layer. The product is shared, source-backed memory that local agents can query without starting every session from zero.

sections.heading: The Architecture Is the Product
sections.text: The best-known agent-memory systems — Mem0/OpenMemory, Zep/Graphiti, Letta — store memory as embeddings in a vector database or as an LLM-extracted graph. You cannot read your own memory, and a model sits inside the…
sections.body: The best-known agent-memory systems — Mem0/OpenMemory, Zep/Graphiti, Letta — store memory as embeddings in a vector database or as an LLM-extracted graph. You cannot read your own memory, and a model sits inside the write path. Link made five architectural commitments that cannot be bolted onto those designs: Memory you can read Every memory is a plain Markdown file. Open it, grep it, git-diff it, back it up. If Link disappeared tomorrow, your memory is still yours. Review-gated writes No durable memory is created without your approval. Agents propose; you decide. Automatic session hooks capture proposals — never facts. No LLM in the memory layer Ingestion and recall are deterministic. An extraction model can hallucinate facts into a knowledge graph; Link's memory layer cannot, because there is no model in the write path. Provably local CI blocks outbound network code in the runtime. The optional semantic models load offline-only after one explicit setup. "Local-first" here is enforced, not promised. Memory that holds when the agent acts A memory you reviewed can carry a rule ( ask command: git push --force , deny write: migrations/** ) that is checked before the agent's tool call, with no model and under a millisecond. Memories about code are re-read against your repository and flagged when the code moved on. Memories surface when the agent opens the file they describe, lnk compile writes reviewed memory into the files every agent already reads, and a receipt proves what reached each session. Recall quality is measured, not asserted: a 1,176-case reproducible benchmark plus a third-party LoCoMo retrieval track, with published miss rates and a CI gate against regressions. See benchmarks/RESULTS.md .

You mainly want a polished human writing app, mobile sync, plugins, and manual note-taking. Hosted app memory You want local files, no cloud account, and MCP access from many desktop agents. You are building a hosted product and need managed APIs, user accounts, dashboards, and cloud-scale operations. Stateful agent runtime You already use agents and need shared memory outside any one runtime. You want an entire agent platform with its own execution loop, hosted state, and deployment model. Temporal business graph You need personal/project memory with explicit review and source-backed Markdown. You need automatic entity extraction, temporal fact invalidation, multi-user business data, and enterprise integrations. Plain file search You want search plus memory lifecycle, graph context, MCP tools, validation, and provenance. You only need grep, ripgrep, or a folder of notes with no agent-memory workflow.

Reviewed memory and compact context are the product surfaces agents use. One wiki, three independent surfaces The web UI, CLI, official skills, and MCP server are separate ways to use the same local files. Closing the viewer does not stop CLI commands, skills, or MCP recall. Public repo versus local memory Link deliberately keeps generated raw/ , wiki/ , and link-demo/ content out of git. The tracked root wiki is scaffolding; python3 link.py demo creates the product-story demo wiki. raw/ Immutable notes, papers, articles, transcripts, images, and PDFs. wiki/sources/ One source page per ingested raw file. wiki/memories/ Preferences, decisions, project facts, and user context. indexes Backlinks, page index, local cache, token index, and optional SQLite FTS. Markdown remains the source of truth. Derived indexes can be rebuilt. Agents maintain the files, but the files stay inspectable in git, Obsidian , or any editor.

sections.body: The lifecycle can run automatically: session hooks inject the memory brief at session start and store proposal-only notes at session end, and when the review backlog grows, briefs nudge the agent to offer a read-only lnk consolidate pass. Every write still requires explicit user approval — automation changes when memory is proposed , never who decides. A memory is a Markdown page with status, scope, visibility, source, review state, optional review_after and expires_at dates, graph links, and local log entries. It can be proposed, remembered, reviewed, updated, archived, restored, explained, or forgotten. Propose Generate candidate memories from chat notes or raw captures without writing durable memory. Approve Save only the memories the user explicitly wants agents to carry forward. Explain Show why a memory exists, whether it is recall-ready, and what graph links support it. Re-check Use review_after when a memory should come back to the inbox after a date instead of staying trusted forever. Expire Use expires_at for temporary context that should leave default recall after a date while staying inspectable. Enforce Give a reviewed memory a rule ( ask or deny on a command, read or write) and the session hook checks it before the agent's tool call; only you can turn a rule on. sections.heading: Smart Query Packets
sections.text: Retrieval is lexical by default (token matching, stemming, SQLite FTS) and optionally hybrid : two local embedding tiers (a tiny static model for instant CLI use, a contextual model for the MCP server) add paraphrase…
sections.body: Retrieval is lexical by default (token matching, stemming, SQLite FTS) and optionally hybrid : two local embedding tiers (a tiny static model for instant CLI use, a contextual model for the MCP server) add paraphrase recall while staying fully offline at query time. Semantic matches are labeled and confidence-capped so agents verify before trusting them; measured results live in benchmarks/RESULTS.md . recall is designed for agents. It returns a compact packet with a recall_capsule , relevant memory, ranked wiki pages, graph context, provenance, budget reports, estimated size, and follow-up actions. Budget tiers keep context predictable: micro : the smallest capsule-first context for quick recall. small : fast, compact context for most questions. medium : more memory and page context for active tasks. large : broader context when the agent needs to plan or compare.

sections.heading: CLI Tour
sections.text: Status, query, brief, and benchmark are the core terminal loop. The CLI is independent of the web viewer. Use lnk start , lnk query , lnk brief , lnk session-end , lnk health , and maintenance commands even when lnk…
sections.body: Status, query, brief, and benchmark are the core terminal loop. The CLI is independent of the web viewer. Use lnk start , lnk query , lnk brief , lnk session-end , lnk health , and maintenance commands even when lnk serve is not running. Agents that support lazy-loaded instructions can also use the official Link skills instead of MCP setup. Use lnk try when you want the shortest proof loop: demo creation, readiness, query proof, brief proof, viewer command, and first agent prompts in one command. Use lnk demo [dir] to create a sample workspace with a few memories, raw sources and wiki pages, so you can try recall, the viewer and the graph without touching your own memory. It refuses to overwrite a directory that is not an earlier demo; --force replaces an earlier demo. Use lnk proof when you want to prove the cross-agent memory loop directly: one clean local workspace, one reviewed memory, and one bounded recall packet shared by CLI, skills, and MCP. Use lnk setup for install day and every upgrade after it: it detects every agent installed on your machine and wires them all — workspace, MCP provisioning, session hooks, and a refresh of any stale Link-owned agent instruction files (a steering file from an older Link can name MCP tools the configured server no longer exposes, sending the agent back to file greps) — in one idempotent command. Use lnk onboard when you want the guided single-agent flow: safe repair, health check, optional first memory, optional project seed, first prompts, and optional agent MCP wiring. If the local viewer is running, /onboard mirrors that flow with copy buttons. Use lnk seed . ~/link from a project directory when you want Link to create a source-backed project page from existing repo context before the first real recall. It scans allowlisted docs/rule files, blocks secret-looking values, and does not create durable memories silently.

sections.body: One rule for the memory knobs. Finding it → --trigger (a phrase that helps task-shaped recall find a recipe). Fencing it → --applies-when (conditions that demote or hide a memory outside its context). Owning it → --scope / --project / --visibility (whose memory it is and who may see it). Replacing it → --supersedes (archive the old claim with lineage; accepts the memory name or its title). Aging it → --review-after / --expires-at . When in doubt, save with none of them — every knob can be added later through review. lnk remember Save a local agent memory. Strong duplicates and likely conflicts are refused unless explicitly allowed. lnk recall Search local memories with recall readiness, project-aware filtering, type filters, and --as-of temporal recall. lnk recipes List saved procedure memories with their triggers and first steps. lnk explain-memory Show provenance, lifecycle, graph links, review issues, and recall readiness. lnk update-memory Merge new text into an existing memory and reset review state. lnk archive-memory Reversibly hide a stale or wrong memory from default recall. lnk forget-memory Permanently delete a memory after explicit confirmation.

sections.text: The most universal pain of multi-agent work: a rate limit hits mid-task, you switch tools, and the first ten minutes go to re-explaining. lnk handoff writes a standalone packet - task, state, next steps - and the next…
sections.body: The most universal pain of multi-agent work: a rate limit hits mid-task, you switch tools, and the first ten minutes go to re-explaining. lnk handoff writes a standalone packet - task, state, next steps - and the next session on any connected agent opens with it: session-start hooks and the MCP first response both carry it, so delivery never depends on the agent thinking to ask. Handoffs expire on their own (48h), are secret-redacted at write time, and never become durable memory unless you promote them through normal review. lnk handoff "Auth refactor: token validation moved, refresh test failing" --task "Auth refactor" --next "Fix refresh test" lnk handoffs # list pending lnk handoffs --clear FILE # after the next session picks it up

Nothing is ever auto-accepted, Link's own instruction sections are excluded, and re-running an import is a no-op for anything already pending, dismissed, or saved. lnk import claude-code # CLAUDE.md + auto-memory lnk import cursor # rules files lnk import codex # AGENTS.md (minus Link's own section) lnk import file --file chatgpt-memories.txt # anything pasted to a file Review at bulk speed when a capture is trustworthy: lnk accept-capture FILE --all accepts every proposal (duplicates and conflicts are skipped and reported, never forced), and lnk delete-capture TARGET --all --confirm clears the whole inbox with dismissals recorded.

sections.body: lnk sync moves reviewed memory between your machines through a git remote you control (a private repo, a homelab bare repo) — no server, no service. By default it writes AGENTS.md plus the agents the repository already has files for; --targets all or a comma-separated list chooses others. lnk compile --global --dry-run lnk compile --global lnk compile --global is for the agents with no session-start hook. It writes your reviewed personal memories (never a project's, and none fenced to a project, path or task) into the file Windsurf, Kiro and Zed read in every session, in one Link-owned block that keeps the rest of the file byte for byte and fits Windsurf's 6,000-character limit for the whole file. For Zed it also writes your personal rules into agent.tool_permissions in ~/.config/zed/settings.json , marked with a comment, and only where you have no permissions of your own; if you do, it prints the block to merge by hand. It never writes through a symlink or inside a git work tree. After that, changing a memory in your personal workspace keeps those files in step. sections.heading: Check Instruction Files
sections.text: lnk stale ~/link --repo . --instructions lnk stale ~/link --repo . --instructions --json lnk stale --instructions checks the repository's own agent instruction files the way lnk stale checks memories: every AGENTS.md ,…
sections.body: lnk stale ~/link --repo . --instructions lnk stale ~/link --repo . --instructions --json lnk stale --instructions checks the repository's own agent instruction files the way lnk stale checks memories: every AGENTS.md , CLAUDE.md and GEMINI.md (nested ones too), .claude/rules , Cursor, Windsurf and Kiro rules, and Copilot's instruction files. It reports three things and changes none of them: Stale references. Paths, scripts, make and just targets, dependencies, variables, local endpoints, runtime versions and package managers the repository once had and no longer does, with the same history rule as memories. In an instruction file a bare filename counts only as a link ( [CLAUDE.md](CLAUDE.md) ); “run main.ts” is an example. A nested file's links are resolved from its own folder. Size limits. Text an agent never reads: Codex stops after 32 KiB of AGENTS.md, counted along the chain from the repository root to each nested file; Windsurf reads 12,000 characters of a rule; Claude Code skips a CLAUDE.md over 4 MiB. Each finding gives the limit and how far over. Longer-than-recommended files (CLAUDE.md over 200 lines, a Cursor rule over 500) are reported as warnings that do not fail the check. Contradictions. Rules in two instruction files, or a rule and a reviewed memory, that cannot both hold (“always use tabs” and “never use tabs”; “2 spaces” and “4 spaces”). Copies of the same rule in AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md are not contradictions, and words inside code, links or names do not count. With the local contradiction model on disk ( lnk semantic --setup --nli ) pairs the word rules miss are added. Link's own compiled block and Link-owned files are skipped: their content comes from memories, which lnk stale checks. Exit codes are the same as lnk stale : 0 nothing found, 1 something to fix, 2 could not check. lnk stale ~/link --wiki lnk stale ~/link --wiki --json lnk stale --wiki checks the compiled wiki against its sources, with no repository needed. It lists pages written before a raw file they rest on was edited (even after the source page itself was refreshed), source pages older than their raw file, source pages whose raw file was deleted, citations to a page that does not exist, pages whose every citation is another wiki page (so nothing they claim reaches raw/ or a memory), and pairs of pages that look like the same concept: a shared name, title or alias, or…

sections.text: lnk backup lnk doctor --fix lnk health lnk status --validate lnk memory-audit lnk compliance-export --output link-audit.json lnk team-sync ~/link lnk snapshot ~/link --output link-snapshot lnk operations lnk benchmark…
sections.body: lnk backup lnk doctor --fix lnk health lnk status --validate lnk memory-audit lnk compliance-export --output link-audit.json lnk team-sync ~/link lnk snapshot ~/link --output link-snapshot lnk operations lnk benchmark "agent memory" lnk rebuild-index lnk rebuild-backlinks lnk stale lnk receipt lnk validate lnk verify-mcp Use lnk backup before broad repair work. Use lnk benchmark when a wiki starts to feel slow or when you want to see how much broad wiki context the bounded packet avoided sending to an agent. lnk status --validate and lnk benchmark both show persistent-cache reuse so you can tell whether Link is rereading every page or reusing unchanged records. Run lnk stale from inside a repository to list memories that describe things the repository no longer has. It checks file paths (with the new name when git recorded a rename), package scripts ( npm run deploy:staging ), make and just targets, dependencies, environment variables and URLs, and two direct contradictions with files the repository checks in: a runtime version the manifests no longer allow (“Python 3.10” when pyproject.toml requires >=3.12 ) and a package manager whose lockfile was replaced by another manager's. Each reference is only reported when the repository shows it once had the thing and no longer does, so prose that merely looks like a filename, a variable or a script stays quiet. On this repository's own documentation plus eight other real repositories, that rule produced no false flags across more than 600 references (exact figures in benchmarks/RESULTS.md ). It also re-reads each memory's code anchors ( path:line symbol , recorded when the memory was written inside a checkout) and reports symbols that were removed. A symbol that only moved within its file is not a finding, and anchors from another repository are never checked here. Claims framed as history (“we dropped Python 3.9”) or as a prohibition (“do not use npm”) are not read as current claims, monorepo workspace manifests count, and links to public documentation are left alone. History answers are cached per commit in the workspace's .link-cache/ , so repeat runs on a large repository are fast. The command changes nothing: it tells you which memories to review. It exits like a linter, so CI and scripts can act on the result. 0 means nothing was flagged, 1 means at least one memory was flagged, and 2 means it could not…

sections.heading: Predictable Agent Workflow
sections.text: Memory arrives on its own. Only some agents support session hooks, so Link also pushes through the one channel every MCP agent shares: the first tool response of a session carries a compact memory brief under…
sections.body: Memory arrives on its own. Only some agents support session hooks, so Link also pushes through the one channel every MCP agent shares: the first tool response of a session carries a compact memory brief under link_session_brief , whatever tool was called — even status . It happens once per session, is skipped when there is nothing to say, is recorded as a retrieval so lnk wins can prove it happened, and is disabled with LINK_MCP_AUTOBRIEF=off . Agents should treat it as context they already have. If Link session hooks are installed for the agent ( lnk connect <agent> --hooks --write ), the startup brief is injected automatically — agents should skip the manual brief call and go straight to bounded task recall. When a brief reports a memory backlog, review(action="consolidate") returns a read-only consolidation plan to walk through with the user. New MCP configs use the slim surface by default so agents see one obvious read tool and one obvious write tool instead of a long menu of overlapping helpers. The full compatibility surface remains available with --surface full . Slim agents should use Link in this order: Call status when connecting or troubleshooting. Call recall with an empty query once at the first substantive turn of a session. Call recall(query, budget="micro") before broad file reads or asking the user to repeat durable context. Call ingest when the user drops files into raw/ . Call remember only after the user explicitly approves durable memory. At session end, call admin(action="session_end") or capture_session to propose memory candidates without saving them silently. Call review for memory inbox, profile, audit, log, receipt, explain, archive, restore, and forget workflows. Change who a memory is shared with through admin(action="set_visibility") , after the user approves. Rules a memory enforces on tool calls are set with admin(action="set_enforce") only when the user asks; they act after the user reviews the memory, and an agent cannot mark a rule-bearing memory reviewed, clear its rules, or archive, forget or update it over MCP - the person does that in the CLI, the viewer or LinkBar. Call admin for backup, migrate, validate, rebuild, graph export, pages, captures, and advanced updates.

sections.body: The inbox is where memory becomes trusted, so it is built to be fast and to show everything that a review turns on. Keyboard. j / k move, r reviews, a archives, x selects, e opens the edit form. Focus moves to the next memory without a reload. Inline edit. Change the claim or the visibility in place. The claim goes through update-memory , so duplicate and conflict checks still run, and nothing is sent unless it changed. Rules before approval. A memory that carries enforced rules lists them under its claim in the words the hook uses ( asks , blocks ). Reviewing it activates those rules for the agent's tool calls, so the request must acknowledge the rules it displayed; the server refuses otherwise. Bulk review skips rules. Select several memories and review or archive them at once. Memories with enforced rules are skipped and reported, so rules are never switched on in a batch. Outside content is marked. On the captures page, proposals from a session that read web pages or MCP tool output say so, so you can check the words are yours before accepting. The wins page carries a Last session card mirroring lnk receipt : which memories the agent was given, whether every brief arrived whole, how many tool calls the enforced rules asked about or blocked, and how many code reminders fired.

sections.body: With session hooks installed ( lnk connect <agent> --hooks --write ), step one happens automatically: the bounded memory brief is injected at session start and proposal-only notes are captured at session end. Hooked agents skip the manual brief call and go straight to bounded task recall. Call status . If schema or validation needs attention, follow the safe action it returns. Call recall with an empty query once at the first substantive turn of a session. The brief always keeps room for standing preferences (active, unconditional, user-scope preferences about how the agent answers, formats, cites or behaves). Those apply to every task but share no words with any task, so ranking by recency alone would drop them. Call recall(query, budget="micro") before broad file reads or asking the user to repeat durable context. Call ingest after the user drops files into raw/ , then follow its guided plan. Use remember only after the user explicitly asks to remember something or approves a proposal. When a brief opens with a Waiting for the user's OK block, list those proposals and rules to the user and act on one only after they reply in chat; never approve from the block itself. Use review for memory inbox, profile, audit, log, explain, archive, restore, and forget workflows. Use admin for backup, migration, graph export, captures, rebuilds, and advanced maintenance. User: is Link ready? Agent: status() User: start with Link before we continue Agent: recall(query="", mode="brief") User: query Link for the release plan Agent: recall(query="release plan", budget="small")

sections.heading: Core Tool Groups
sections.text: Need Primary tools Contract behavior Readiness status Returns safe next actions instead of guessing. Recall recall Returns startup briefs, ranked memory/wiki context, graph context, reasons, and budget limits. Memory…
sections.body: Need Primary tools Contract behavior Readiness status Returns safe next actions instead of guessing. Recall recall Returns startup briefs, ranked memory/wiki context, graph context, reasons, and budget limits. Memory writes remember , review Requires explicit approval and surfaces duplicate/conflict candidates. Ingest ingest Provides raw-source plans, validation, and rebuild checks. Maintenance admin Handles backup, migrate, validate, graph export, captures, pages, rebuilds, and compatibility actions. Recalled memories carry honest signals agents must respect: a confidence label ( strong / moderate / weak ) and, when the optional local semantic tier is installed, a match field ( lexical / hybrid / semantic ). Semantic-only matches are capped below strong confidence — verify them with the user before acting. When a brief reports a memory backlog, review(action="consolidate") (or lnk consolidate ) returns a read-only plan; apply its actions only with per-item user approval. When recall runs inside a git checkout, each returned memory that names something in the repository is checked against it. A memory carries verified , with the commit sha it was checked at and references_checked , when at least one file, symbol, script, target, dependency, variable or version it names was found in place and nothing it names is gone. Naming things the repository never had is not evidence either way. A memory that names something the repository once had and no longer has carries stale_paths , one entry per finding, with the path , the reason , the successor when git recorded a rename, and evidence , and the packet's agent_guidance tells the agent to check the memory against the current code before relying on it. Claims framed as history or as a prohibition (“we dropped Python 3.9”, “do not use npm here”) are not checked as present-tense claims, and links to public documentation are facts about the world, not about the repository. The checks share a short time budget and a history cache per commit; a memory whose checks did not finish in time is left unmarked, never called verified on partial evidence. Memories that name nothing checkable carry neither key; a missing key is normal, not a warning. A memory written or updated inside a git checkout that names a repository file along with a code symbol found in that file gets anchors . Each anchor records where the symbol was,…

sections.heading: Memory Receipt
sections.text: Link records that each brief and recall happened in .link-usage.json at the workspace root. That lets you see what actually reached your agent, not just what is stored. lnk receipt (or review(action="receipt") over MCP)…
sections.body: Link records that each brief and recall happened in .link-usage.json at the workspace root. That lets you see what actually reached your agent, not just what is stored. lnk receipt (or review(action="receipt") over MCP) groups those events into sessions: runs of retrievals with no gap longer than 30 minutes. For each session it shows: when the session started and ended; the project; the surfaces it came through ( hook , mcp , cli ); each session brief, with how many memories it carried, roughly how many tokens it cost, and whether a budget cut it short; how many recalls there were; any guard reminders; every memory the agent was given, with a count; for each hook injection, whether it arrived whole, was cut off, or never arrived (and unverified when the agent left no transcript to check); the enforced-rule checks that ran before tool calls, and whether each asked for the user's OK or blocked the call; the code reminders: memories surfaced because the agent read or edited the file they describe. Every memory in the receipt comes with the command to explain it and the command to forget it. lnk receipt ~/link --sessions 3 lnk receipt ~/link --json The ledger never records query text, answers, or anything from the conversation, only that a memory was used and which one. It is machine-local, excluded from sync, capped at a ring of recent events, and switched off with LINK_USAGE=off . Events recorded before 5.0 have no surface or size, and the receipt says so instead of guessing.

sections.heading: Point-in-Time and Typed Recall
sections.text: Every memory is a dated file with its lifecycle recorded ( date_captured , supersedes , superseded_by , archived_at ). That makes “what was true then” an exact reconstruction, not a guess. recall accepts two optional…
sections.body: Every memory is a dated file with its lifecycle recorded ( date_captured , supersedes , superseded_by , archived_at ). That makes “what was true then” an exact reconstruction, not a guess. recall accepts two optional arguments: as_of ( YYYY-MM-DD ) answers with the memories that were active on that date, following supersede lineage backwards. memory_type ( preference , decision , fact , procedure , project , note ) narrows recall to one kind. Either one routes the call to memory recall, where lineage and types are recorded. Nobody types dates into a question, so a plain time phrase in the query does the same job. Link resolves it to a date and drops the phrase from the text it ranks: last week/month/quarter/year , this week/month/quarter/year , 3 weeks ago , in March , in 2025 , as of 2026-03-31 , and the deliberately vague back then or originally , which it reads as about a quarter ago. Phrases anchored to an event ( before the migration ) are not resolved to a date, and the event name stays in the query. Resolution is deterministic and offline; unrecognised phrasing leaves recall unchanged. recall(query="which database did we use last quarter?") recall(query="deploy day", as_of="2026-03-31") recall(query="formatting", memory_type="preference")

sections.heading: Write Rules
sections.text: Agents should treat Link memory as durable state, not scratch space. Do not call remember unless the user explicitly asks to remember something. Use admin action propose_memories for transcripts, long notes, or…
sections.body: Agents should treat Link memory as durable state, not scratch space. Do not call remember unless the user explicitly asks to remember something. Use admin action propose_memories for transcripts, long notes, or uncertain context. If a write returns duplicate_candidates , update the existing memory instead of creating another one. If a write returns conflict_candidates , explain the conflict and ask the user before overriding. If a write returns possible_contradictions , tell the user which stored memories the new one may contradict and offer to supersede or archive the old one. The memory is already saved; the flag asks for review, it does not block. Use review_after for memories that should be re-checked, and expires_at for temporary context. Never review, clear, archive or update a memory that carries enforced rules. Only the user does that, in the viewer or the CLI, after seeing the rules; the MCP surface refuses, and the hook asks before an agent runs those commands itself. Contradiction flags (optional). Word rules catch contradictions that share structure, such as “uses X” against “no longer uses X”, or two different version numbers. After lnk semantic <dir> --setup --nli , a small local natural-language-inference model also reads meaning. What it checks. On each remember , it scores the new claim against at most five stored memories whose subject words overlap with it by at least 30%. The overlap gate is what keeps it from reading two unrelated project rules as a contradiction. What it adds. A pair scored at 0.9 or higher gets a review_note on the new memory, and the write result includes possible_contradictions , with the name , title and probability of each flagged memory. What it never does. It never blocks a save and never runs during recall. A missing or failing model cannot break a write. LINK_NLI=off turns it off. Proposals from transcripts and session-end captures are filtered before anything reaches the inbox. Only the user's own words are mined. Text the agent harness injects is dropped: system reminders, command output, sub-agent turns and compaction summaries. So are the shapes that were never memory: instructions for the work at hand (“do not edit any files”) with no standing-rule framing; requests to the agent; goals for this one conversation; throwaways and hypotheticals; other people's habits; anything tied to today or tomorrow;…

title: Security
label: Security
lead: Link has no hosted backend, no telemetry, no external API calls, and no cloud account requirement. The safety model is local files, explicit writes, and inspectable provenance.

sections.heading: Privacy Model
sections.text: No telemetry in the installed CLI, MCP server, local web UI, or wiki runtime. No hosted backend. No external API calls from serve.py or link-mcp . Raw sources and generated wiki pages are ignored by git by default.…
sections.body: No telemetry in the installed CLI, MCP server, local web UI, or wiki runtime. No hosted backend. No external API calls from serve.py or link-mcp . Raw sources and generated wiki pages are ignored by git by default. SQLite search, when available, is an in-memory derived index. Markdown remains the source of truth. Optional semantic recall stays local: embedding models load offline-only at recall time (only the explicit lnk semantic --setup may fetch a model, once), embeddings live in plain JSON under .link-cache/ , and CI blocks outbound network code in the runtime. Automatic session hooks store proposal-only notes; no durable memory is written without explicit review. Transcript extraction skips tool calls and tool outputs, and it drops text the harness writes with the user's role but the user never typed: subagent reports, slash-command expansions, local command output, interruption markers, compaction summaries and messages from other sessions. Secret-shaped values are redacted before a capture is written to disk; the inbox still names what was redacted so you know to rotate it. Session handoffs are delivered to the next session on any agent, framed as notes from a previous session rather than instructions. A handoff carrying injection-shaped instructions is labelled, and the agent is told to show it to you and not act on it until you confirm it is yours. Retrieval observability is local-only and minimal. So you can answer "are my agents actually using this?", Link records that a brief or recall happened, when, and which memory names came back — in .link-usage.json at the workspace root. It never records your queries, the answers, the conversation, or anything about the machine; it is bounded to the most recent events; it is excluded from lnk sync (behavior is not memory, and it never leaves this machine); and it is switched off entirely with LINK_USAGE=off . The public GitHub Pages documentation may use lightweight analytics to understand install interest. It does not run inside Link, read local wiki data, or capture source/memory content.

sections.heading: Enforced Rules
sections.text: A reviewed memory can carry rules that are checked before the agent's tool calls. Because a rule changes what an agent may do, only a person turns one on or off. Over MCP an agent cannot approve, clear, archive or…
sections.body: A reviewed memory can carry rules that are checked before the agent's tool calls. Because a rule changes what an agent may do, only a person turns one on or off. Over MCP an agent cannot approve, clear, archive or update a memory that carries rules; the viewer activates rules only when the review request repeats the rules it displayed, and never in bulk. The session hook also asks for your OK before an agent runs Link's own review, enforce, archive or forget commands, or edits a memory file directly, so an agent cannot quietly loosen its own constraints. Rules are checked through each agent's own pre-tool hook: Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, Gemini CLI, Antigravity, Copilot, Windsurf and Kiro. Some of those agents can only allow or block a call. There, an ask rule holds the call: it is blocked, the agent is told to ask you in chat, and lnk approve <id> (or Approve once in LinkBar) lets that exact call through once within ten minutes. lnk approve shows the call before granting it. The approval is single-use and covers that call only, including what it writes: approving one patch does not let a different patch to the same file through. Approving stays with you: lnk approve is one of the governance commands the hook holds however it is spelt (through a variable, a substitution or a git alias too), and the approvals file lives in the workspace's .link-cache/ , which the hook treats like the memory files. A command the hook cannot read, such as eval "$c" , waits for your OK. What the hook is, and is not: it runs as you, inside the agent's own permissions, and reads each command as the shell will. That stops a mistaken or talked-into call and the usual disguises of one. It is not a sandbox: an agent set on escaping it can write a program that does the forbidden thing, or edit its own hook settings, and no check running as the same user can prevent that. For an agent you do not trust, run it in a container or a separate account.

The importer rejects, and reports, pages that are not visibility: team , not active, symlinks (a symlink in a shared repo can point at any file on your disk), or that carry a secret-shaped value or an injection-shaped instruction. lead: Large local wikis should stay usable because agents receive budgets, graph overviews open bounded first, search uses SQLite FTS when available, and unchanged pages are reused from the persistent cache.

sections.heading: Practical Promise
sections.text: Link is local personal memory software. The expected sweet spot is a real user's working wiki: hundreds to thousands of Markdown pages, raw sources, durable memories, and graph links. The product is designed so agents…
sections.body: Link is local personal memory software. The expected sweet spot is a real user's working wiki: hundreds to thousands of Markdown pages, raw sources, durable memories, and graph links. The product is designed so agents do not need to enumerate that whole corpus for normal work. Search SQLite FTS5 is used when Python provides it. Link stores a derived FTS sidecar under .link-cache/ so unchanged wikis can reuse the search table across process starts. Cache reuse Persistent page-cache records let repeated runs reuse unchanged parsed pages instead of rereading everything after every command. If SQLite FTS is unavailable, Link falls back to a token index and reports that backend in status and benchmark output. Graph Large graphs open as a bounded high-signal overview first. Users can search, filter, focus neighborhoods, or explicitly load more when they need it. Agent context MCP and CLI query packets use micro, small, medium, and large budgets. Agents read the recall capsule first, then follow-up actions instead of dumping every page into the model.

sections.body: The important scale behavior is not "can Link list every page?" It is "does the default agent and UI path stay bounded?" Surface Default behavior Expansion path recall Returns a budgeted context packet plus a tiny hybrid-ranked recall capsule. Use follow-up actions for more memory, search, context, or graph detail. admin(action="graph_summary") Returns a bounded topic or high-degree graph neighborhood. Increase limit/depth or request the full graph only when needed. Local graph UI Starts capped with sparse labels and motion limits for large wikis. Use type filters, node search, focused neighborhoods, fullscreen, and explicit all-data loading. All pages Lists a bounded window grouped by page type. Use paging, search, and type filters instead of scrolling the whole wiki. Health Shows readiness, validation, interrupted writes, backend, and cache reuse. Run repair commands only when health points to a specific issue; doctor uses the parsed page cache for backlink checks.

sections.body: Recall quality is measured too, not just speed: the repo ships a 1,176-case recall benchmark and a third-party LoCoMo retrieval track with reproduction commands — see benchmarks/RESULTS.md . Use lnk benchmark on your real wiki. It reports cache time, persistent-cache reuse, search backend, search/query timing, graph payload shape, value evidence, and recommendations. The value section compares broad wiki body text with the bounded query packet so you can see whether Link is reducing context-budget waste. lnk benchmark "agent memory" lnk health lnk status --validate From a source checkout, use a synthetic 10k-page check without touching your real wiki: python3 scripts/smoke_large_wiki.py --pages 10000 The smoke script prints the generated wiki path, the local viewer command, and graph URLs so you can inspect browser behavior manually.

Keep private raw sources and local wiki/log.md out of Git; use snapshot , team-sync , and compliance-export for reviewable sharing paths.

sections.heading: Current Limits
sections.text: Link is not pretending to be an enterprise search cluster. These are the current boundaries to understand before betting a huge corpus on it: Indexes are local and process-owned. Very large wikis still use memory…
sections.body: Link is not pretending to be an enterprise search cluster. These are the current boundaries to understand before betting a huge corpus on it: Indexes are local and process-owned. Very large wikis still use memory proportional to the page/index size. The SQLite FTS index is built locally from wiki pages rather than maintained as a separate hosted service. The local HTTP viewer is for personal loopback use, not a multi-user hosted deployment. Full graph exports are intentionally not the default for large wikis. Use bounded graph summaries first. At tens of thousands of pages and beyond, persistent on-disk indexing and chunked graph loading become the next engineering frontier. The near-term direction is clear: preserve the plain Markdown storage model while making cache, search, graph, and validation paths more incremental over time. sections.body: Every claim links to a source. Confidence tags make uncertainty visible. log.md records wiki operations. Pages mature from seed to established. Agents should use slim recall first, then follow up with admin graph/context actions only when the compact packet is insufficient. The local web viewer has no runtime dependencies beyond Python stdlib. The wiki is plain Markdown, so it works with git, Obsidian, and normal editors.
